posts.title: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: Skipping Most of the Context
posts.subtitle: A cheap indexer picks the few thousand tokens actually worth attending to
posts.summary: Full attention costs grow quadratically with context length, so at 100K+ tokens most of that compute scores tokens the model will barely use. Sparse attention schemes like DeepSeek's fix this with a cheap 'lightning indexer' that picks a small, relevant subset of past tokens before the expensive attention math ever runs.

slides.title: Attention gets quadratically more expensive, not linearly
slides.body: Standard self-attention compares every token to every other token. Double the context length and you roughly quadruple the attention compute — the single biggest cost driver once contexts pass 100K tokens.
bullets: Full attention cost scales as O(L²) in sequence length L
At long context, attention — not the feed-forward layers — dominates latency and cost
Most of those pairwise comparisons contribute almost nothing to the output

slides.title: Long context makes the waste obvious
slides.body: For any given query token, only a handful of past tokens are actually relevant to predicting the next word — a citation, a variable definition, a earlier turn in the conversation. Full attention still scores every single one.
bullets: A 128K-token document might have only a few thousand tokens relevant to any one query
Dense attention pays full price to discover that most tokens don't matter
Naive fixes (fixed sliding windows, strided patterns) throw away tokens by position, not relevance

slides.title: A lightning indexer scores relevance before attention runs
slides.body: DeepSeek Sparse Attention adds a small, cheap side-network — the 'lightning indexer' — that assigns each past token a lightweight relevance score against the current query. Only the top-scoring tokens are kept for the real, expensive attention computation.
bullets: The indexer is deliberately lightweight — its own cost is a small fraction of full attention
Every past token gets scored, but only the top-k highest-scoring ones proceed to real attention
Real attention then runs over that small selected set, not the full context
Effective cost drops from O(L²) toward O(L·k), where k is fixed regardless of context length

slides.title: Trained by distillation, not bolted on after the fact
slides.body: A sparse selector trained from scratch tends to silently drop tokens the model actually needed. DeepSeek's approach instead warm-starts from a model that still uses dense attention, then trains the sparse student to match what the dense teacher would have attended to.
bullets: Start from a checkpoint trained with ordinary dense attention
Train the indexer + sparse attention path to approximate the dense model's attention pattern
This keeps quality close to dense attention instead of degrading once tokens get dropped
The indexer effectively learns 'which tokens would dense attention have cared about?'

slides.title: Worked example: a long document query
slides.body: Picture a 128K-token codebase pasted into context, and a query token asking about a function's behavior partway through generation.
bullets: The indexer cheaply scores all prior tokens against that query — the function's own definition, its call sites, and nearby comments score high
Unrelated boilerplate elsewhere in the file scores low and gets skipped
Real attention then runs only over that small relevant subset — a fraction of the full 128K tokens
The output should look close to what full dense attention over all 128K tokens would have produced

slides.title: Three attention strategies at long context

rows: Top-k tokens chosen by learned relevance
Depends on indexer quality; mitigated by distillation

slides.title: Where this doesn't pay off
slides.body: Sparse attention isn't free — the indexer itself adds a pass over the whole sequence, and a poorly trained one can miss tokens the model genuinely needed, with failures that are easy to miss in normal evals.
bullets: Below a certain context length, the indexer's overhead isn't worth the savings
An undertrained indexer creates a silent recall problem: dropped tokens the model needed but never got to see
Distillation quality against the dense teacher is what determines whether sparsity is safe to ship
It optimizes inference and long-context training cost — it doesn't reduce total parameter count

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Full attention's O(L²) cost makes long context expensive — most token comparisons don't matter
A cheap lightning indexer scores every past token, then keeps only the top-k for real attention
Training the sparse path to imitate a dense-attention teacher (distillation) is what preserves quality
Below a length threshold, or with an undertrained indexer, sparsity isn't worth the tradeoff

questions.prompt: Why does full self-attention become the dominant cost at long context lengths?
options: Because feed-forward layers scale worse than attention
Because attention cost scales quadratically (O(L²)) with sequence length, while other layers scale roughly linearly
Because the tokenizer becomes slower on long inputs
Because KV cache memory doesn't affect compute cost
questions.explanation: Self-attention compares every token to every other token, so its cost grows as O(L²) in sequence length L. Feed-forward layers scale closer to linearly, so past a certain length, attention dominates total compute and latency.

questions.prompt: What does the 'lightning indexer' do in DeepSeek Sparse Attention?
options: It compresses the model's weights to reduce memory
It cheaply scores every past token's relevance to the current query, so only the top-k proceed to full attention
It replaces the tokenizer with a faster one
It reorders tokens by position before training
questions.explanation: The indexer is a lightweight side-network that assigns a relevance score to every past token for the current query. Only the highest-scoring top-k tokens go on to the expensive real attention computation, cutting effective cost from O(L²) toward O(L·k).

questions.prompt: Why is the sparse attention path typically trained by distilling from a dense-attention model, rather than trained from scratch?
options: Distillation is required by the Lean proof checker
It makes the model smaller in total parameter count
Training from scratch is impossible with mixture-of-experts layers
It teaches the indexer to approximate what a dense model would have attended to, avoiding silently dropped tokens that hurt quality
questions.explanation: An indexer trained from scratch risks silently dropping tokens the model actually needs, degrading quality in ways that are hard to catch. Warm-starting from a dense-attention checkpoint and distilling against it keeps the sparse selection close to what full attention would have chosen.

posts.title: Attention Sinks: Why the First Few Tokens Hold a Cache Together
posts.subtitle: A streaming LLM trick that keeps perplexity from collapsing at any length
posts.summary: Sliding-window KV caches keep memory bounded but collapse in quality the moment the very first tokens get evicted. Keeping a handful of those initial tokens permanently in the cache — as 'attention sinks' — fixes this with almost no extra cost, letting a model serve an effectively unbounded conversation.

slides.title: Why can't a chatbot just run forever?
slides.body: Every transformer keeps a growing key/value cache for every token it has seen. Left alone, that cache eventually eats all your memory — so serving systems cap it. The naive fix for capping it quietly breaks the model.
bullets: KV cache grows with every generated token
Production serving needs a hard memory ceiling
The obvious fix — a sliding window — has a hidden failure mode

slides.title: Sliding windows collapse the moment token 0 leaves
slides.body: The intuitive fix is to only keep the most recent N tokens in the KV cache and drop the rest, like a ring buffer. It works right up until the buffer wraps around and evicts the very first tokens of the sequence — at which point output quality falls apart.
bullets: Drop oldest tokens once the cache hits its size limit
Fine as long as eviction hasn't reached the start of the sequence
The instant token 0 is evicted, perplexity spikes and generation degrades

slides.title: Softmax has nowhere to put 'no attention'
slides.body: Attention scores for every query must sum to 1 across whatever keys are visible. If a token has nothing useful to attend to, the softmax still has to spend its probability mass somewhere — and models learn to dump that leftover mass onto the first few tokens, regardless of their content.
bullets: Softmax output always sums to 1 — there's no 'attend to nothing' option
Early tokens absorb huge attention scores unrelated to their meaning
Researchers call this an attention sink: a release valve baked in by training
Evicting the sink tokens removes that valve, and scores redistribute badly

slides.title: Cache the sinks, slide the rest
slides.body: The fix keeps the KV cache split into two parts: a small fixed set of sink tokens from the very start of the sequence that are never evicted, plus a normal sliding window of the most recent tokens. Everything in between is dropped.
bullets: Reserve a few slots (often just 4) for the first tokens — never evict them
Slide the remaining budget over the most recent tokens as normal
No retraining or architecture change needed on many existing models
Position indices are reassigned within the cache, not tied to original sequence position

slides.title: A support bot running for 100,000 turns on a 2,048-token budget
slides.body: Imagine a chat agent with a hard 2,048-token KV cache, deployed for a support session that runs to 100,000 tokens over the day.
bullets: Plain sliding window: stable until token 2,049 pushes out token 0-3, then quality visibly degrades for the rest of the session
Sink + window: tokens 0-3 stay pinned as sinks; tokens 2,044 onward slide normally; quality stays flat all day
The sink tokens don't need to be semantically special — even the BOS token works
Memory footprint is identical to the plain sliding window — the fix is where you evict from, not how much you keep

slides.title: Three ways to bound a KV cache
What this trick does not give you
slides.body: Attention sinks buy stability, not memory. It's easy to mistake a stable streaming session for a model that 'remembers' the whole conversation.
bullets: Content from the evicted middle is genuinely gone — the model can't recall it
This is a stability fix, not a substitute for real long-context or retrieval
Too few sink tokens (e.g. just 1) can still be unstable; the right count is model-dependent
For tasks that truly need old context back, pair this with RAG or a summarization step, not sinks alone

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Sliding-window KV caches cap memory but collapse when they evict the first tokens
Early tokens absorb disproportionate attention because softmax must sum to 1 — an 'attention sink'
Pinning a handful of sink tokens while sliding the rest restores stability at near-zero extra cost
It fixes generation quality for infinite streams — it does not restore lost mid-conversation memory

questions.prompt: Why does a plain sliding-window KV cache degrade once it evicts the first few tokens?
options: Those tokens contain the model's system prompt
Softmax attention must sum to 1, and models learn to dump excess attention onto early tokens as a release valve
The tokenizer reassigns different IDs after eviction
GPU memory becomes fragmented at that point
questions.explanation: Because softmax scores must sum to 1 across visible keys, models learn to route leftover attention mass to a few fixed early tokens regardless of content. Remove those tokens and the model has nowhere well-calibrated to put that mass, so outputs degrade.

questions.prompt: What's the key structural change attention sinks make to a sliding-window cache?
options: It doubles the cache size to hold more recent tokens
It retrains the model with a new loss function
It permanently reserves a few slots for the earliest tokens while the rest of the cache slides normally
It compresses old tokens into a single summary vector
questions.explanation: The cache is split into a small fixed pool of never-evicted sink tokens plus a normal sliding window for recent tokens — no compression or retraining required.

questions.prompt: What can attention sinks NOT do?
options: Keep perplexity stable across very long streams
Work on existing models without fine-tuning
Restore information from tokens that were evicted from the middle of the conversation
Bound the KV cache to a fixed memory footprint
questions.explanation: Attention sinks fix generation stability, not memory — content evicted from the middle of the stream is genuinely gone. Recovering it requires retrieval or summarization, not sink tokens.

posts.title: BDH-CQ: A 150M Model Breaks the ARC-AGI Cost Frontier
posts.subtitle: Recurrent latent reasoning beats verbalized chain-of-thought on cost per solved task.
posts.summary: Pathway's BDH-CQ solves ARC-AGI-1 puzzles by updating a fixed-size recurrent memory and iterating in latent space instead of writing out chain-of-thought text. At 150M parameters it hits 29.5% pass@2 for about $0.0007 per task, landing beyond the previously reported cost-accuracy frontier for the benchmark.

slides.title: A 150M-Parameter Model Just Broke a Cost Frontier
slides.body: Pathway's BDH-CQ reasons inside a recurrent latent state instead of writing out its thinking — and it's dramatically cheaper per solved ARC-AGI-1 task than anything reported before it.

slides.title: Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Gets Expensive Fast
bullets: Most reasoning models solve hard puzzles by verbalizing step-by-step thought — every extra token of reasoning is extra compute you pay for at inference time.
ARC-AGI-1 tests abstract visual pattern induction from a handful of examples; frontier LLMs have needed heavy scaling (bigger models, longer traces) to make real progress on it.
That leaves a cost-accuracy frontier: plot accuracy against $/task and most systems that get more accurate also get proportionally more expensive.

slides.title: Think in a Recurrent Memory, Not in Text
bullets: BDH-CQ is built on Dragon Hatchling (BDH), Pathway's post-transformer recurrent architecture where neuron-like units communicate through low-rank interactions.
Instead of a growing KV cache, it keeps a fixed-size recurrent associative state that gets updated as each in-context demonstration is read.
At query time it doesn't emit an intermediate chain-of-thought — it solves the task through iterative computation inside that latent state, then produces the answer directly.

slides.title: An 'Effort' Knob That Adds Latent Iterations, Not Tokens
bullets: The model exposes LOW vs. HIGH effort settings — more effort means more rounds of internal latent iteration on the same fixed-size memory, not longer written output.
Moving from LOW to HIGH effort raised pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1 from 21% to 29.5%.
Because the extra computation stays in latent space rather than generated tokens, the cost curve for more 'thinking' is far flatter than it is for verbalized chain-of-thought.

slides.title: What More Effort Buys You

rows: More latent iterations; ~0.85 H200-GPU-seconds and ~$0.0007 per task

slides.title: Solving a Grid-Transformation Puzzle
slides.body: An ARC-AGI task shows a handful of input/output grid pairs that share a hidden transformation rule, then asks the model to apply that rule to a new input grid.
bullets: BDH-CQ reads each demonstration grid and folds it into its recurrent associative state — no text description of the rule is ever generated.
At the new query grid, it runs its latent iterations to converge on an answer grid directly from that compressed state.

A standard LLM attempting the same task would typically verbalize a hypothesis about the rule in text first ('the shape rotates 90° and recolors...'), burning output tokens whether or not that hypothesis is right.

slides.title: Where This Approach Runs Into Limits
bullets: No verbalized reasoning trace makes it harder to inspect why the model reached a given answer — there's no chain-of-thought to audit.
The result is demonstrated on ARC-AGI-1, not the harder ARC-AGI-2 successor or general open-domain reasoning — it's a specialist result, not a general-purpose reasoning replacement.
Training leans on a curated mixture of ARC-style data (RE-ARC, ConceptARC, ARC-Heavy and similar augmentations) — the efficiency gain is tied to a task family with that kind of structure.
At 150M parameters it isn't a general chat or knowledge model; it trades broad capability for narrow, cheap iterative reasoning.

slides.title: The Big Idea
bullets: Reasoning cost doesn't have to scale with output tokens — BDH-CQ moves the 'thinking' into a fixed-size recurrent latent state instead of generated text.
An effort knob that adds latent iterations (not tokens) gives a cheaper way to trade compute for accuracy than longer chain-of-thought.
It's a data point for a broader post-transformer direction (Dragon Hatchling) where memory and inference share the same computational fabric rather than being bolted together.

questions.prompt: What does BDH-CQ do instead of writing a verbalized chain-of-thought to solve an ARC-AGI-1 task?
options: It iterates inside a fixed-size recurrent latent state and outputs the answer directly
It samples multiple text completions and votes on the majority answer
It retrieves the answer from a lookup table of past ARC solutions
It fine-tunes its weights on each new puzzle before answering
questions.explanation: BDH-CQ folds each demonstration into a recurrent associative memory and solves the query through iterative latent computation — never generating an intermediate text reasoning trace.

questions.prompt: Going from LOW to HIGH effort in BDH-CQ mainly changes what?
options: The number of output tokens it generates
The number of latent iteration rounds on its fixed-size memory
The number of model parameters that get activated
The size of the training dataset used
questions.explanation: Effort in BDH-CQ controls how many rounds of internal latent iteration the model runs on its recurrent state — not how much text it writes, which is why the cost curve stays flat compared to verbalized reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why is BDH-CQ's result described as breaking a 'cost-accuracy frontier' rather than just a new accuracy record?
options: It's the first system to ever solve any ARC-AGI-1 task
It reaches its accuracy at a lower reported cost per task than any prior plotted system at that accuracy or better
It has more parameters than any competing model
It was the first model trained without any ARC-style data
questions.explanation: A cost-accuracy frontier plots the best accuracy achieved at each price point; BDH-CQ's 29.5% pass@2 at roughly $0.0007/task lands beyond every previously reported point on that frontier, not just above one specific model's accuracy.

posts.title: DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813: Preview Graduates to Flagship
posts.subtitle: Selectable reasoning effort, a bolted-on speculative decoder, and native support for OpenAI's Responses API.
posts.summary: DeepSeek shipped V4-Pro-0813, the official production release superseding the V4-Pro preview: three selectable reasoning-effort levels replace the old fixed thinking budget, a new DSpark speculative decoding module speeds up generation, and the model now natively supports OpenAI's Responses API — all on the same 1M-token, unchanged-parameter base.

slides.title: DeepSeek's Flagship Leaves Preview
slides.body: After roughly four months in preview, DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 is the official production release — same base model, several production-focused upgrades bolted on.

slides.title: A Preview Tag Doesn't Survive Contact With Production
bullets: DeepSeek-V4-Pro had been running as a preview build for months while frontier competitors kept shipping — a preview label makes teams hesitant to build production agents on top of it.
The preview shipped with a single fixed thinking budget, which is a blunt instrument: the same reasoning depth for a one-line autocomplete and a multi-file refactor.
Agentic and tool-calling workloads exposed rough edges that only show up under real production traffic, not static benchmarks.

slides.title: What 0813 Actually Changes
bullets: Replaces the single fixed thinking budget with three selectable reasoning-effort levels — low, high, and max — so callers pick depth per request.
Adds a DSpark speculative decoding module attached to the existing V4-Pro-preview model structure, aimed at faster token generation without changing the base weights.
Adds native support for OpenAI's Responses API, easing integration for teams already building against that interface.
Model name, parameter count, and the 1-million-token context window are unchanged from the preview.

slides.title: Speculative Decoding, Bolted On Rather Than Retrained
bullets: Speculative decoding works by having a cheap draft step propose several tokens ahead, which the full model then verifies in parallel — accepted tokens are 'free', rejected ones fall back to normal generation.
DSpark is attached to the same V4-Pro-preview weights rather than requiring a retrained base model, which is why the released parameter count and context window didn't move.
This mirrors a broader industry pattern: ship a speculative-decoding layer as an add-on to cut latency/cost on an already-trained model instead of re-training for speed.

slides.title: Preview vs. 0813

rows: Adds native OpenAI Responses API support

slides.title: Picking Effort Per Request
slides.body: A team running a coding agent harness can now route work by task shape instead of paying one fixed reasoning cost for everything.
bullets: Quick autocomplete-style edits get routed at 'low' effort — fast, cheap, good enough for a single-file change.
A gnarly multi-file refactor or a failing-test debugging loop gets routed at 'max' effort, trading latency and cost for deeper reasoning.

Official pricing starts at $0.435 / $0.87 per 1M input/output tokens on a cache miss, with peak/off-peak rates added a few days after launch — worth checking the current rate card before committing usage at scale.

slides.title: Read the Benchmark Fine Print
bullets: Third-party benchmark write-ups on 0813's exact SWE-bench Verified score don't fully agree with each other — treat any single quoted percentage with some skepticism until you've checked the eval harness it came from.

Independent agentic-coding leaderboards that score full open-ended agent loops (not just single-patch generation) place it further from the top than patch-style benchmarks suggest — strong at some task shapes, weaker at others.
Pricing tiers (peak/off-peak) were introduced shortly after launch, so a quoted price from launch day can already be stale.

slides.title: The Big Idea
bullets: 'Preview to GA' upgrades are often about production ergonomics (effort controls, API compatibility, latency) more than raw capability — the base model here didn't even change size.
Speculative decoding modules like DSpark are a cheap way to cut latency/cost on an already-trained model without a full retrain.
Always sanity-check third-party benchmark claims against multiple sources — coding-agent evaluations especially disagree depending on harness setup.

posts.title: HNSW: How Vector Search Skips Scanning Everything
posts.subtitle: A layered small-world graph trades a sliver of recall for enormous query speed.
posts.summary: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph-based index most vector databases use for approximate nearest-neighbor search. By stacking sparse-to-dense graph layers and greedily walking toward the query, it turns a linear scan over millions of embeddings into a handful of graph hops — at the cost of memory, exactness, and cheap deletes.

slides.title: Nobody Scans 10 Million Embeddings Per Query
slides.body: Exact nearest-neighbor search over embeddings costs O(N) per query. HNSW is the graph structure most vector databases use to get sub-linear search instead.

slides.title: Brute-Force kNN Doesn't Scale
bullets: Exact k-nearest-neighbor search compares the query vector against every stored vector — cost grows linearly with the number of embeddings.
A RAG system with 10M+ chunks and multiple queries per second can't afford a full scan per request and still feel interactive.
The fix is approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search: give up a small, tunable amount of recall in exchange for order-of-magnitude faster queries.

slides.title: Small-World Graphs, Stacked Like a Skip List
bullets: HNSW builds several graph layers stacked on top of each other; each vector is randomly assigned a top layer via an exponentially decaying probability, so higher layers have far fewer nodes.
A search starts at the sparse top layer and greedily walks toward whichever neighbor is closest to the query.
Once no neighbor at the current layer is closer, the search drops down one layer and keeps walking — narrowing in fast at the top, then refining at the bottom where the full graph lives.
It's the same idea as a skip list, but the 'sorted order' is replaced by vector similarity.

slides.title: Three Knobs, One Recall/Speed/Memory Triangle
bullets: M — the max number of neighbor edges per node per layer (commonly in the teens to tens). Higher M raises recall and memory use, and slows insertion.
efConstruction — the candidate list size used while building the graph. Higher gives a better-connected graph at slower build time.
efSearch — the candidate list size used at query time. Higher raises recall at the cost of query latency, and can be tuned per query without touching the index.

slides.title: HNSW vs. the Alternatives

rows: High — graph edges plus vectors, usually in RAM
No cheap delete; tends to need periodic rebuilds
Simpler to build, generally weaker recall than HNSW

slides.title: Walking a Query Through a 10M-Vector Index
slides.body: A RAG system has embedded 10 million document chunks at 768 dimensions and built an HNSW index with M=32, efConstruction=200.
bullets: A user's query embedding arrives. Search enters at the top layer, which might hold only a few hundred nodes.
It greedily hops toward the query by vector distance, drops a layer once nothing closer is available, and repeats — layer by layer, down to layer 0 where every vector lives.
At the bottom layer it expands a candidate list of size efSearch (say, 100) and returns the top-10 nearest chunks — typically in single-digit milliseconds instead of scanning all 10 million vectors.

slides.title: Where HNSW Bites You in Production
bullets: Memory-hungry: the graph edges plus the full vectors normally need to sit in RAM for speed, so 10M x 768-dim floats already cost multiple gigabytes before graph overhead.
No cheap delete: removing a node breaks its neighbors' edges, so most implementations tombstone deleted vectors and periodically rebuild rather than delete in place.
Recall is probabilistic, not guaranteed: the greedy walk can get stuck in a local optimum and miss a true nearest neighbor, especially rare edge cases.
Aggressive metadata filtering that shrinks the candidate pool too much can tank recall — filtering interacts badly with a graph built for the unfiltered space.

slides.title: The Big Idea
bullets: HNSW replaces a linear scan with a layered graph walk — sparse layers narrow the search fast, dense layers refine it.
Three knobs (M, efConstruction, efSearch) let you trade recall, speed, and memory against each other — and efSearch is tunable per query.
It's the default ANN index in most vector databases today, but IVF and hybrid indexes still matter when memory or update-heavy workloads make HNSW's tradeoffs a bad fit.

questions.prompt: Why do vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search instead of exact kNN at scale?
options: Exact kNN is illegal to use in production systems
Exact kNN's cost grows linearly with the number of vectors, which is too slow for large, interactive workloads
ANN always returns more accurate results than exact search
Exact kNN can only be run on GPUs
questions.explanation: Brute-force kNN compares the query against every stored vector — O(N) per query. ANN methods like HNSW trade a small amount of recall for far faster, sub-linear queries.

questions.prompt: In HNSW, what happens as a search moves from the top graph layer toward the bottom?
options: The search restarts from scratch at each layer with no memory of progress
It greedily narrows in using sparse, long-range connections first, then refines with the denser bottom layer
It switches to a brute-force scan at the bottom layer
Layers are used only during index construction, not during search
questions.explanation: Top layers are sparse, so the walk covers large distances fast; the search drops a layer whenever it can't get closer, ending at the dense bottom layer for fine-grained refinement — similar to how a skip list narrows in on sorted data.

questions.prompt: Which HNSW parameter can be changed per query, without rebuilding the index, to trade latency for recall?
options: M
efConstruction
efSearch
Vector dimensionality
questions.explanation: efSearch controls the candidate list size used at query time and can be raised or lowered per query. M and efConstruction are baked into the graph at build time and require reindexing to change.

posts.title: Agent Memory: What Survives Between Turns
posts.subtitle: Why long-running agents need more than a bigger context window.
posts.summary: Long-running agents outgrow their context window fast. This post breaks down the three-tier memory model — working, episodic, and long-term — the write/read/compaction loop that keeps it running, and the real tradeoffs (cost, staleness, retrieval noise) that decide when memory helps and when it's dead weight.

slides.title: Agent Memory: What Survives Between Turns
slides.body: A long-running agent's context window is a whiteboard, not a filing cabinet — every eviction risks losing something it still needed.

slides.title: The Context Window Is a Leaky Bucket
slides.body: Even a large window fills fast once tool results, file diffs, and stack traces get appended verbatim turn after turn.
bullets: A 200K-token window (~150K words) sounds huge until every tool result and file diff is appended in full.
The naive fix — drop the oldest messages first — deletes exactly where the user's original constraints usually live.
Result: an agent that confidently violates a rule it was told 40 turns ago, not out of carelessness but because it literally can't see it anymore.

slides.title: Three Tiers, Not One Memory
slides.body: MemGPT's framing is useful: treat the context window like RAM and an external store like disk, paging facts in and out instead of hoping everything fits.
bullets: Working memory: the live context window — fast to read, free, but capacity-limited.
Episodic memory: a running summary of what happened, written after each task and compacted over time.
Long-term / semantic memory: durable facts and preferences stored outside the window (vector store or key-value profile), pulled back in only when relevant.

slides.title: Two Paths: Write and Read
slides.body: The system does real work on both ends of a turn, not just at read time.
bullets: Write path: after each turn, an extraction call pulls out durable facts ('DB is Postgres, not MySQL') and appends them to storage — not the raw transcript.
Read path: before the next turn, retrieve the top-k relevant memories by embedding similarity or keyword match and inject only those into the prompt.
Compaction loop: periodically summarize older episodic entries into fewer, denser ones so storage doesn't grow without bound.

slides.title: Picking a Strategy
slides.body: No single strategy wins everywhere — the right one depends on session length and how sparse the useful facts are.

rows: Chat where old context rarely matters
One extra LLM call per compaction

slides.title: A Coding Agent Hits Its Limit
slides.body: The difference between memory tiers shows up exactly when the window is under pressure.
bullets: Turn 3: the user says, 'don't touch the /legacy endpoint, other teams depend on it.'
Turn 180: context is 90% full of test output and diffs; that original sentence has long since scrolled out of the window.
With memory: the instruction was extracted as a durable fact at turn 3, stored externally, and retrieved again at turn 180 because the next edit touches a file that imports /legacy.
Without memory: the agent refactors /legacy anyway — not from carelessness, but because it can no longer read what it was told.

slides.title: When Memory Makes Things Worse
slides.body: Memory is a tradeoff, not a free upgrade — it adds failure modes of its own.
bullets: Stale facts: a preference from three weeks ago can be actively wrong today; memory needs expiry or versioning, not just accumulation.
Retrieval noise: pulling back ten 'relevant' memories for a simple question adds tokens and can distract the model more than it helps.
Extra latency and cost: every write path is another LLM call — for a one-shot Q&A agent, that overhead buys nothing.
Memory poisoning: a wrong fact written once gets faithfully retrieved and repeated until someone corrects it.

slides.title: The Takeaway
bullets: Working memory (the context window) is fast but finite — treat it as cache, not storage.
Write summaries and extracted facts to long-term memory, not raw transcripts.
Retrieve selectively: more memory injected isn't automatically better recall.
Skip long-term memory entirely for short, single-session tasks — the overhead isn't worth it there.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of simply truncating the oldest messages when a context window fills up?
options: It increases token cost
It can silently drop constraints or instructions the user gave earlier
It always improves latency
It corrupts the model's weights
questions.explanation: Truncating oldest-first assumes old messages matter least, but early turns often carry the constraints (like 'don't touch this endpoint') that later turns depend on.

questions.prompt: In the MemGPT-style OS-paging analogy, what does the external memory store correspond to?
options: CPU cache
RAM
Disk in a virtual-memory system
A network socket
questions.explanation: MemGPT treats the LLM's limited context window like RAM and pages information in and out of a slower, larger external store — analogous to disk in OS virtual memory.

questions.prompt: Which task is the worst fit for bolting a long-term memory system onto an agent?
options: A multi-day coding session across many files
A customer-support bot that should remember prior tickets
A one-shot question-answering call with no follow-up
A research agent tracking findings across dozens of searches
questions.explanation: A single-shot interaction has nothing to remember for later — the write/read overhead of a memory system only pays off across multiple turns or sessions.

posts.title: FlashAttention: Fusing Attention to Skip the Memory Round-Trip
posts.subtitle: IO-aware tiling and an online softmax mean the N×N attention matrix never has to touch slow GPU memory.
posts.summary: FlashAttention rewrites attention as a single fused GPU kernel that tiles Q/K/V into on-chip SRAM and uses an online softmax so the full N×N attention matrix never has to be written to slow HBM. It computes exact attention — identical output to the naive algorithm — while training measurably faster and scaling memory linearly instead of quadratically with sequence length.

slides.title: FlashAttention: Fusing Attention to Skip the Memory Round-Trip
slides.body: Self-attention is quadratic in sequence length — but the hidden cost is worse: every step reads and writes a full N×N matrix through slow GPU memory. FlashAttention rewrites the computation so that matrix never leaves the chip.

slides.title: Standard attention is memory-bound, not compute-bound
slides.body: Naive attention computes QKᵀ, writes the whole N×N score matrix to HBM, reads it back for softmax, writes the result again, then reads it once more to multiply by V.
bullets: An A100's HBM moves data at roughly 1.5–2TB/s; its on-chip SRAM is close to an order of magnitude faster — every unnecessary HBM round-trip costs far more wall-clock time than the matmul itself.
The N×N score matrix grows quadratically: at sequence length 8K that's a 64-million-entry matrix per head, written and re-read multiple times before a single attention output exists.
This is why long-context training runs out of memory well before it runs out of raw FLOPs — the bottleneck is data movement, the same underlying issue that makes single-token LLM decoding slow.

slides.title: Tile Q/K/V into SRAM and never materialize the full matrix
slides.body: FlashAttention fuses the matmul, mask, softmax, and second matmul into one GPU kernel, processing blocks of queries against blocks of keys/values that fit entirely in fast on-chip SRAM.
bullets: For each query block it loops over key/value blocks, computing partial scores and immediately folding them into the output — the full N×N matrix is never written to HBM at all.

An 'online softmax' keeps a running max and running sum per query row, rescaling the accumulated output as each new block arrives — algebraically identical to computing softmax over the whole row at once.

In the backward pass it recomputes attention from the small saved statistics instead of storing the full matrix — extra compute traded for far less memory traffic, since compute is cheap relative to HBM bandwidth.

slides.title: Walking through an 8K-token sequence
slides.body: Sequence length 8,192, block size 128 — naive attention versus FlashAttention's tiling.
bullets: Naive attention: an 8,192×8,192 score matrix per head — about 67 million floats (~268MB in fp32) written to and read from HBM before the output exists.
FlashAttention: loops through 64 key/value blocks of 128 tokens each, holding at most one 128×128 tile (~64KB) in SRAM at any time.

After each tile, the running softmax max/sum for every query row updates and the partial output rescales — by the 64th tile the result is numerically the exact softmax over all 8,192 keys, computed without ever holding the full matrix at once.

slides.title: The win is memory traffic, not new math — and it compounds in v2
slides.body: FlashAttention computes exact attention, identical output to the naive algorithm — the speedup comes entirely from cutting HBM reads/writes, and FlashAttention-2 pushes the same idea further with better GPU work partitioning.

rows: Only ~25–40% of an A100's theoretical peak FLOPs/s utilized
Most kernel time goes to moving the N×N matrix through HBM, not computing
3x faster GPT-2 training (seq 1K); 15% faster end-to-end BERT-large than the MLPerf 1.1 record; 2.4x on Long-Range Arena
Fused kernel + tiling removes the N×N HBM round-trip entirely
~2x faster than FlashAttention; up to 230 TFLOPs/s on A100 (73% of peak); 225 TFLOPs/s (72% model FLOPs utilization) end-to-end training
Better parallelization across thread blocks/warps and fewer non-matmul ops in the inner loop

slides.title: It doesn't cut FLOPs, and short sequences barely notice
slides.body: FlashAttention is exact and purely an I/O and kernel-fusion optimization — it changes zero math, so it isn't always the right lever to pull.
bullets: At short sequence lengths the N×N matrix already fits comfortably in SRAM-sized chunks with little wasted bandwidth — the speedup shrinks and may not justify a specialized kernel.
It doesn't reduce the underlying O(N²) FLOP count of exact attention — for very long contexts you still need a genuinely sub-quadratic or sparse/linear scheme, not just a faster exact one.

Recomputing the attention matrix in the backward pass adds real extra FLOPs versus caching it — a good trade only because compute is cheap and memory bandwidth is the actual bottleneck on modern GPUs.
It requires a custom fused kernel tied closely to specific GPU architectures — portability isn't automatic, which is why FlashAttention-2 and -3 exist as separate hardware-tuned releases.

slides.title: Same math, radically fewer memory round-trips
bullets: FlashAttention computes exact attention — no approximation, same output as the naive algorithm, just reorganized to be IO-aware.
Tiling plus online softmax mean the O(N²) score matrix is never fully materialized in HBM — memory use drops from quadratic to linear in sequence length.
Reported gains: 3x GPT-2 training, 15% BERT-large end-to-end, 2.4x Long-Range Arena (FlashAttention); ~2x further and up to 73% of A100 peak FLOPs (FlashAttention-2).
It's a foundation, not a cure-all — it doesn't reduce attention's FLOP count, and its benefit scales with how memory-bound your sequence length actually is.

questions.prompt: What is the primary bottleneck FlashAttention targets in standard attention?
options: Reads/writes of the N×N score matrix between GPU HBM and on-chip SRAM
The number of floating-point operations in QKᵀ
Network bandwidth between GPUs in distributed training
The numerical precision of the softmax function
questions.explanation: Standard attention is memory-bound: it repeatedly writes and reads the full N×N score matrix through slow HBM. FlashAttention doesn't change the FLOP count — it removes those HBM round-trips.

questions.prompt: How does FlashAttention avoid ever materializing the full N×N attention matrix?
options: It tiles Q/K/V into SRAM-sized blocks and uses an online softmax to incrementally accumulate the output
It approximates softmax with a cheaper linear function
It prunes low-attention-score tokens before computing softmax
It stores the matrix in a compressed quantized format
questions.explanation: Online softmax keeps a running max and sum per query row so each new key/value block's contribution can be folded into the output immediately — mathematically identical to full softmax, computed one block at a time.

questions.prompt: Which statement about FlashAttention's tradeoffs is accurate?
options: It recomputes attention in the backward pass to trade extra compute for less memory traffic, and does not reduce attention's underlying O(N²) FLOP count
It approximates attention scores, trading a small amount of accuracy for speed
It only works for inference, not training
It replaces softmax with a hardware-friendly sigmoid
questions.explanation: FlashAttention is exact, not approximate. Its speedup comes purely from cutting memory traffic — including recomputing rather than storing the attention matrix during backprop — not from doing less math overall.

FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning (Dao, 2023)

posts.title: Speculative Decoding: Guessing Tokens to Skip the Wait
posts.subtitle: A tiny draft model guesses ahead so the big model only has to verify, not generate, one token at a time.
posts.summary: Speculative decoding speeds up LLM generation by having a small draft model guess several tokens ahead, then letting the large target model verify all of them in a single parallel forward pass. A rejection-sampling correction guarantees the output distribution is identical to plain decoding — it's a pure latency win, not a quality tradeoff.

slides.title: Speculative Decoding: Guessing Tokens to Skip the Wait
slides.body: LLM generation is slow not because GPUs are weak, but because they sit mostly idle waiting on memory. Speculative decoding fixes that by having a small model guess ahead.

slides.title: Autoregressive decoding wastes the GPU, not the CPU
slides.body: Generating one token means a full forward pass through every weight, streamed from HBM into compute. The arithmetic takes nanoseconds; loading the weights takes milliseconds.
bullets: A 70B model in fp16 is roughly 140GB of weights read from memory for every single token generated.
At batch size 1, that forward pass uses a tiny fraction of the GPU's available FLOPs — the bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not compute.
This is why batch-1 generation from a large model can crawl even on top-tier hardware: the GPU spends most of its time waiting on memory, not computing.

slides.title: Draft cheap, verify in parallel, keep the same output
slides.body: A small 'draft' model autoregressively guesses the next several tokens — fast, since it's tiny. The big 'target' model then checks all of them in a single forward pass, which is nearly free per extra token because it's compute-bound, not memory-bound.
bullets: Verification uses rejection sampling: accept a draft token with probability min(1, p_target(x) / p_draft(x)).
If rejected, resample from the residual distribution (p_target − p_draft)⁺, normalized — this keeps the final output mathematically identical to sampling from the target model alone.
Net effect: the same memory-bound pass that used to yield 1 token now often yields several, because the expensive weight read happens once for many candidate tokens instead of once per token.

slides.title: Walking through one verification step
slides.body: Draft model proposes 4 tokens for the prompt 'The capital of France is'; the target model checks all 4 in one pass.
bullets: Draft guesses: 'Paris', 'and', 'it', 'is' — the target computes true probabilities for all 4 positions simultaneously, not one at a time.
Tokens 1–3 ('Paris', 'and', 'it') pass the accept test — the target agreed strongly, since these are near-deterministic continuations.
Token 4 ('is') is rejected — the target resamples its own token there instead (e.g. 'known'), and the draft restarts guessing from that point.
Result: 3 tokens accepted for the cost of roughly one target forward pass, instead of 4 sequential passes.

slides.title: Where the speedup actually shows up
slides.body: The technique's introducing paper measured a 2-3x wall-clock speedup on T5-XXL with no change to output quality, because verification guarantees the same distribution as plain sampling.

rows: Speedup near the top of the range
High agreement between draft and target — most guesses accepted
Higher entropy means more rejections and more resampling
Serving is already compute-bound at scale, so there's less idle compute for 'free' verification

slides.title: When speculation doesn't pay off
slides.body: Speculative decoding trades extra compute for lower latency — that trade isn't free.
bullets: Needs a second model resident in GPU memory (the draft) — real VRAM overhead, though drafts are typically 10-20x smaller than the target.
A poorly-matched draft (different tokenizer, very different training distribution) gets rejected constantly — you pay for guesses that never land, with no speedup.
High-temperature, high-diversity sampling lowers acceptance rates, since the target's true distribution disagrees with the draft more often.

Gains shrink as serving batch size grows, since verification stops being 'free' once the GPU is already compute-saturated — the technique matters most for low-batch, latency-sensitive serving, not high-throughput batch offline inference.

slides.title: The core idea, in one line
bullets: Let a cheap model guess several tokens ahead, then let the expensive model check them all in one memory-bound pass instead of many.
Rejection sampling guarantees the output is statistically identical to plain decoding — this is a speed trick, not a quality tradeoff.
Biggest wins: low-batch, latency-sensitive serving with predictable text. Smallest wins: high-batch throughput serving or highly creative sampling.

questions.prompt: Why is single-request (batch=1) LLM decoding usually memory-bound rather than compute-bound?
options: Because attention is quadratic in sequence length
Because every token requires reading the full model weights from memory, while only a small amount of arithmetic happens per byte read
Because GPUs don't have enough FLOPs for transformers
Because tokenization runs on the CPU
questions.explanation: At batch=1, one forward pass streams the entire weight matrix from memory but performs comparatively little arithmetic on it — so time is dominated by moving bytes, not computing. This is the exact bottleneck speculative decoding attacks: verifying several tokens in one pass amortizes that memory read over more output.

questions.prompt: What guarantees that speculative decoding produces the exact same output distribution as normal decoding from the target model?
options: The draft model is trained to be identical to the target model
A modified rejection-sampling accept/resample rule that corrects for any mismatch between the draft and target probabilities
Both models are run with temperature = 0
The target model only checks the last proposed token
questions.explanation: A draft token is accepted with probability min(1, p_target/p_draft), and on rejection the algorithm resamples from the leftover probability mass (p_target − p_draft)⁺. This correction — not similarity between the models — is what makes the sampled output statistically indistinguishable from vanilla decoding.

questions.prompt: In which serving scenario does speculative decoding help the LEAST?
options: A single user chatting with a large model on a dedicated GPU
Autocomplete for repetitive boilerplate code
A high-throughput server already running many concurrent requests at a large batch size
Generating a long, mostly deterministic form letter
questions.explanation: At large batch sizes the GPU is already compute-bound, so there's little idle compute left for 'free' verification passes — the memory-bound gap speculative decoding exploits has mostly closed. It shines most for low-batch, latency-sensitive serving.

posts.title: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning: NVIDIA Bets on Speed Over Size
posts.subtitle: 31.6B params, 3.6B active, ~670 tok/s — built for the boring parts of agent loops
posts.summary: NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, an open-weight hybrid Mamba-MoE-attention model that matches gpt-oss-120b on intelligence benchmarks with about a quarter of the parameters, hitting ~670 tokens/sec. It's paired with NeMo Switchyard, a router that sends routine agent steps to small fast models and only escalates to bigger ones when needed.

slides.title: A Model Built for Throughput, Not Bragging Rights
slides.body: On August 11, 2026, NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Lightning — the direct successor to Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B — alongside NeMo Switchyard, a router for splitting agent work across models by task.
bullets: Open weights, OpenMDW-1.1 license
Hybrid Mamba-2 + MoE + attention architecture
1M token context window

slides.title: Most Agent Steps Don't Need a Genius
slides.body: A long agent loop spends most of its steps on tool calls, result validation, and delegating to subagents — repetitive work where raw reasoning power is wasted and latency is what actually hurts.
bullets: Frontier models are overkill for 'call this tool, check this JSON'
Latency compounds across dozens of loop iterations
Running a huge model for every step burns GPU time you didn't need to spend

slides.title: 31.6B Total, Only 3.6B Active
slides.body: Lightning mixes Mamba-2 state-space layers, mixture-of-experts layers, and attention layers, so only about 11% of its 31.6B parameters fire on any given token.
bullets: 31.6B total params, 3.6B active per token
Mamba-2 handles long-range state cheaply; attention layers stay for precision
1M token context; NVFP4-quantized weights push throughput to ~670 tokens/sec in NVIDIA's pre-release tests

slides.title: Matching a Model 4x Its Size
bullets: Lightning reaches comparable benchmark scores at roughly a quarter of the total parameters

slides.title: Switchyard: Routing Steps, Not Whole Requests
slides.body: NeMo Switchyard sits in front of an agent harness and assigns each workflow step to the cheapest model that can handle it.
bullets: Step: 'call the search tool and parse results' → routed to Lightning
Step: 'decide the overall plan' → routed to a larger reasoning model
Only the steps that need it pay the big-model latency and cost

slides.title: Open, But Not the Smartest Model in the Room
slides.body: NVIDIA published the training data and recipes alongside the weights — unusually transparent for a model this capable — but Lightning is explicitly optimized for speed and cost, not frontier reasoning.
bullets: Good fit: high-volume, repetitive agent execution steps
Bad fit: complex multi-step planning or novel reasoning tasks
Available on Hugging Face and ModelScope under OpenMDW-1.1

questions.prompt: Why does Lightning only activate 3.6B of its 31.6B parameters per token?
options: It's a dense model that was pruned after training
It mixes MoE layers (only some experts fire) with Mamba-2 and attention layers
It quantizes weights to 4-bit precision
It caches previous activations instead of recomputing them
questions.explanation: The hybrid architecture routes each token through only a subset of MoE experts, so most of the parameter count sits idle for any given token — that's what keeps active compute low while total capacity stays high.

questions.prompt: What problem does NeMo Switchyard solve?
options: It compresses the model for edge deployment
It routes individual agent workflow steps to the model best suited for each one
It fine-tunes Lightning on customer data
It converts weights between quantization formats
questions.explanation: Switchyard sends routine, repetitive steps (tool calls, validation) to fast small models like Lightning, and escalates only the steps that genuinely need more reasoning power to bigger models.

questions.prompt: What's the honest limitation of Nemotron 3.5 Lightning?
options: It has no context window to speak of
It's closed-weight and can't be self-hosted
It's not the strongest model on complex reasoning — it trades some intelligence for speed
It only works with NVIDIA GPUs and no other hardware
questions.explanation: Lightning is designed to match a much larger model's benchmark scores at a fraction of the size and cost, but that trade favors throughput on repetitive tasks over pushing the frontier on hard reasoning.

posts.title: ARIS: Catching a Research Agent's Overconfident Claims
posts.subtitle: A reviewer from a different model family checks the executor's work before it ships
posts.summary: ARIS (Autonomous Research via Adversarial Multi-Agent Collaboration), from Shanghai Jiao Tong University, pairs an executor agent (e.g. Claude) with a reviewer from a different model family (e.g. GPT) to catch unsupported claims in long-running autonomous research. A three-stage claim-auditing layer cross-checks every manuscript statement against a ledger of raw evidence before the paper is allowed to move forward.

slides.title: When a Research Agent Convinces Itself It Succeeded
slides.body: ARIS (arXiv:2605.03042) tackles a specific failure mode in long-horizon autonomous research agents: results that look complete and well-supported, but aren't.
bullets: Open-source; built by a Shanghai Jiao Tong University team
Runs on top of coding agents like Claude Code
Community users have taken ARIS-produced papers through to conference acceptance

slides.title: 'Plausible Unsupported Success'
slides.body: A long-running research agent writes its own report of what it did. If nothing checks that report against the actual evidence, the agent's framing of its own results becomes the paper's framing — errors and all.
bullets: A claimed result can be incomplete, misreported, or just inherited from how the executor described its own work
Self-refinement by the same model rarely catches this — it's the model's own blind spot
The failure looks like a finished, credible paper, which is what makes it dangerous

slides.title: Adversarial Review, Across Model Families
slides.body: ARIS's core idea: have an executor model drive the research forward, but hand every intermediate artifact to a reviewer built by a different lab.
bullets: Executor (e.g. Claude) proposes experiments, writes code, drafts claims
Reviewer (e.g. GPT) critiques those artifacts independently
Different training data and architecture means the reviewer is less likely to share the executor's specific blind spots

slides.title: Three Layers: Execute, Orchestrate, Verify
bullets: Execution layer — 65+ reusable Markdown-defined skills plus a persistent research wiki for reuse across runs
Orchestration layer — five end-to-end workflows with adjustable effort settings and configurable reviewer routing
Assurance layer — a claim ledger plus a three-stage audit: integrity verification, result-to-claim mapping, and claim auditing against raw evidence

slides.title: Tracing a Claim Back to the Log File
slides.body: The executor drafts: 'Method X improves accuracy by a notable margin over the baseline.' Before that line ships, the assurance layer maps it back to the actual evaluation run.
bullets: Claim ledger links the sentence to the specific experiment that produced it
Auditor checks the raw eval output — not the executor's summary of it
If the numbers don't support the phrasing, the paper gets kicked back for revision before a human ever sees it

slides.title: Same-Model Refinement vs. Cross-Model Review

rows: More often — different training, different failure modes
Ledger cross-checks claims against raw logs

slides.title: Where It Helps — and Where It Doesn't
slides.body: ARIS raises the bar for evidential support in agent-written research, but it isn't a substitute for expert judgment on genuinely novel claims.
bullets: Good fit: catching overstated or misreported claims in routine experimental work
Weak fit: judging whether a truly novel idea is significant — that still needs a human
Cost: every review round runs two models instead of one, which adds up on long research loops

questions.prompt: What is 'plausible unsupported success' in ARIS's framing?
options: A model that refuses to attempt a task
A research agent's report that looks complete and credible but whose claims aren't actually backed by the evidence
A benchmark score that's too high to be believable
A paper rejected for formatting errors
questions.explanation: The danger isn't an agent that obviously fails — it's one that produces a convincing-looking result whose supporting evidence is incomplete, misreported, or just inherited from the agent's own framing.

questions.prompt: Why does ARIS use a reviewer from a different model family instead of having the executor review itself?
options: Different-family models are cheaper to run
Same-model self-refinement tends to share the same blind spots as the model that made the mistake
It's required by conference submission rules
Cross-model review runs faster than self-review
questions.explanation: A model checking its own work is unlikely to catch errors that come from its own training biases or reasoning patterns. A differently-trained reviewer is more likely to flag exactly those errors.

questions.prompt: What does ARIS's assurance layer actually check a claim against?
options: The executor's own written summary of what happened
A general knowledge base of prior published results
The raw evidence and logs, via a claim ledger that maps each stated claim back to its source
A vote among multiple reviewer models
questions.explanation: The claim ledger and result-to-claim mapping trace each sentence in the manuscript back to the actual experimental output — not the executor's own description of it — which is what catches claims that drift from the evidence.
