posts.title: StreamPI: Robot Vision Without the Frame-by-Frame Reset
posts.subtitle: One instruction, many frames, constant-cost inference
posts.summary: StreamPI adds temporal reasoning to single-frame vision-language-action robot models without adding a single new parameter, by caching past frames' key/value representations and anchoring attention to the language instruction. On real-robot tasks and the LIBERO benchmark it beats its base model, π0.5, on exactly the tasks single-frame models struggle with: precision and memory-dependent manipulation.

slides.title: A robot policy that forgets everything every frame
slides.body: Most vision-language-action (VLA) models process one camera frame at a time. Each frame is a fresh inference call with no memory of the frame before it — fine for reflexive tasks, brittle for anything that needs continuity.

slides.title: Single-frame models can't do memory-dependent tasks
slides.body: Picking up a cup you can currently see is easy for a single-frame policy. Picking up a cup that briefly left the frame, or tracking which of two similar objects you already grasped, requires remembering what happened a few steps ago — something a stateless per-frame model structurally cannot do.
bullets: Spatial-precision tasks suffer when a single glimpse is ambiguous
Memory-dependent tasks fail outright with no cross-frame state
Naively feeding a whole video window blows up inference cost per step

slides.title: Instruction-anchored attention, cached across time
slides.body: StreamPI treats each (camera frame, language instruction) pair as one atomic unit: bidirectional attention fuses vision and language inside that pair, while causal attention runs across pairs over time — so the instruction stays a persistent semantic anchor as frames stream in.
bullets: Past frames' key/value tensors are cached, not recomputed
Inference cost per new frame stays constant regardless of episode length
Zero new parameters — it's a training/attention scheme, not a bigger model

slides.title: Random-interval training closes the sim-to-real timing gap
slides.body: Training on perfectly regular frame intervals teaches a policy timing assumptions that real robots break — camera jitter, variable control loop latency, and network delay all desynchronize frame arrival on real hardware.
bullets: Random-interval streaming training exposes the model to irregular frame timing during training
This closes the gap between synchronous training and asynchronous real-robot deployment
StreamPI inherits π0.5's pretrained weights directly via LLM length extrapolation — no retraining from scratch

slides.title: Worked example: a two-cup swap task
slides.body: Instruction: 'put the red cup where the blue cup was, and the blue cup where the red cup was.' A single-frame policy re-reads the scene every step and can lose track of which cup already moved. StreamPI's cached KV state carries the swap's progress forward, so the policy doesn't have to re-infer intent from a single ambiguous frame.
bullets: Single-frame π0.5: prone to repeating or skipping a step when objects look similar
StreamPI: attention over cached past frames disambiguates 'already moved' from 'not yet moved'
Same underlying weights — the difference is purely the streaming attention scheme

slides.title: StreamPI vs. its single-frame base model
slides.body: Reported on real-robot manipulation and the LIBERO simulation benchmark, StreamPI consistently outperforms π0.5 on the task categories that need temporal context, while matching it on purely reactive tasks.

slides.title: Why this matters beyond robotics
slides.body: The core trick — cache what you've already attended to instead of recomputing it, and use random timing perturbation to make training match deployment reality — is a pattern that shows up anywhere a model has to reason over a live, irregular stream rather than a fixed batch.
bullets: Streaming KV caching turns a per-frame model into a temporally-aware one for free
Instruction-anchoring keeps long-horizon intent stable across many attention steps
Training-time timing noise is a cheap way to buy real-world robustness

questions.prompt: What does StreamPI add to a single-frame VLA model to give it temporal reasoning?
options: A larger transformer with more layers
A streaming attention scheme that caches past frames' key/value representations, with zero new parameters
A separate memory network trained from scratch
A longer context window filled with raw pixel history
questions.explanation: StreamPI's core idea is architectural, not a bigger model: it caches KV representations from past timesteps and uses instruction-anchored attention across them, adding no new parameters.

questions.prompt: Why does StreamPI use random-interval streaming training instead of fixed, regular frame intervals?
options: To reduce the total number of training examples needed
To make the model robot-brand agnostic
To close the gap between synchronous training and the irregular frame timing of real-robot deployment
To compress the model for edge devices
questions.explanation: Real robots deliver frames at irregular intervals due to jitter and latency. Training with randomized intervals exposes the model to that irregularity ahead of time, instead of assuming a perfectly regular schedule it won't see at deployment.

questions.prompt: On which kind of task does StreamPI show the clearest advantage over its single-frame base model π0.5?
options: Purely reactive tasks with no history dependence
Tasks that require spatial precision or remembering earlier steps
Tasks with no camera input
Text-only instruction following
questions.explanation: StreamPI's gains show up specifically on spatial-precision and memory-dependent manipulation — exactly the cases where a stateless single-frame policy has no way to carry context forward.

posts.title: Contextual Retrieval: Fixing RAG's Broken Chunks
posts.subtitle: Prepend a sentence of context to every chunk before embedding — cache away the cost.
posts.summary: RAG chunks lose the surrounding context that gave them meaning, which is why retrieval so often misses the right passage. Contextual Retrieval fixes this by having an LLM write a short situating blurb for each chunk before it's embedded and indexed — and uses prompt caching to keep that step cheap. Stacked with hybrid BM25 and reranking, measured failure rates dropped from 12.85% to 4.74%.

slides.title: Why RAG misses the answer that's sitting right in the doc
slides.body: Split a document into chunks and each chunk loses the surrounding context that told the reader what it was about. The embedding never learns what it never saw.

slides.title: A chunk torn out of its document loses meaning
bullets: A 200-token chunk that says "the company's revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter" doesn't say which company or which quarter once it's separated from the rest of the filing.
The embedding model only ever sees that one chunk's text — it can't infer what's sitting a page earlier or later.
The result: semantically relevant chunks rank low because the vector representing them is under-specified, not because the search is broken.

slides.title: The fix: have an LLM situate each chunk before it's embedded
slides.body: For every chunk, feed the whole document plus that one chunk to an LLM and ask for a short blurb explaining what the chunk covers and where it sits in the document. Prepend that blurb to the chunk, then embed and index the combined text instead of the raw chunk.
bullets: Prompt pattern: "give a short succinct context to situate this chunk within the overall document, for the purposes of improving search retrieval."
The generated context (roughly 50-100 tokens) is prepended before both embedding and keyword indexing — it's a preprocessing step, not a new embedding model.
Works with any embedding model or vector store already in use.

slides.title: The trick that makes it affordable: prompt caching
bullets: Naively, contextualizing every chunk means resending the FULL document once per chunk — a 100-chunk document means paying for that document 100 times over.

Process chunks document-by-document instead of in random order: the first chunk pays full price to write the document into a prompt cache, every later chunk from that same document reads it back at a steep discount.
Measured on 737 chunks across 9 codebases: $9.20 in input tokens without caching vs. $2.85 with it — a 69% cost cut for identical output.
The cache window only needs to last a few minutes — just long enough to walk through one document's chunks before moving to the next.

slides.title: Each layer stacks on top of the last
bullets: Contextual embeddings alone cut the failure rate roughly 40%; adding hybrid BM25 search on top brings it to about 47%; reranking on top of both reaches roughly 63% fewer failed retrievals than plain baseline RAG.

slides.title: What a generated context blurb actually looks like
slides.body: For a chunk pulled from a differential-fuzzing codebase, the situating step produced: "This chunk contains the module documentation and initial struct definition for a differential fuzzing executor. It introduces the DiffExecutor struct that wraps two executors (primary and secondary) to run them sequentially with the same input, comparing their behavior for differential testing." That ~100-token blurb gets prepended before embedding — so a query like "how does the differential fuzzer compare two executors" now matches on words the raw chunk never contained.

slides.title: When it's not worth the extra LLM calls
bullets: It's an extra LLM call per chunk at index time — for a corpus of atomic records with no natural document boundary (a flat FAQ list, a product catalog), the caching trick doesn't apply and cost climbs fast.
If chunks are already self-contained and short, the added context is just extra tokens diluting the embedding rather than helping it.
Hybrid search adds latency (roughly 50ms) and reranking adds more (roughly 100-200ms) per query — fine for a chat interface, tight for a sub-100ms budget.
Contextual chunks aren't a one-time cost: re-embedding is required every time the chunking strategy or the underlying documents change.

slides.title: The pattern in one sentence
bullets: Chunks fail retrieval because they're read out of context — give the embedding a sentence of context back, and failures drop by roughly half.
Process document-by-document and lean on prompt caching, or the fix costs more than the problem it solves.
Stack it: contextual embeddings, then hybrid BM25, then reranking — each layer adds a real gain for a fraction of the previous layer's cost.

questions.prompt: Why does prepending document-level context to a chunk before embedding help retrieval?
options: It makes the chunk shorter and faster to embed
It restores information the chunk lost when it was split out of its document, so the embedding captures what the chunk is actually about
It replaces the need for a vector database
It removes the need for keyword search entirely
questions.explanation: A chunk's own text often doesn't say what company, document, or section it belongs to. The generated context fills that gap before the text becomes a vector — it isn't about speed or replacing other components.

questions.prompt: Why does processing chunks document-by-document (instead of in random order) matter for cost?
options: It's required by the embedding model's API
It lets multiple documents get batched into one LLM call
It lets the full document stay in a prompt cache so only the first chunk from a document pays full price, while later chunks from the same document read it back at a steep discount
It avoids hitting rate limits on the vector database
questions.explanation: Prompt caching keys off repeated prefix content. Running through one document's chunks back-to-back means that document body is served from cache instead of resent, which is what turned $9.20 into $2.85 in the measured example.

questions.prompt: In the measured Pass@10 results, which single addition took the failure rate from 12.85% to 7.66%?
options: Switching to a larger embedding model
Contextual embeddings alone
Increasing the chunk size
Adding more chunks per query
questions.explanation: Contextual embeddings alone accounted for that drop, roughly 40% fewer failures, before hybrid BM25 or reranking were even added on top.

posts.title: UrbanGround: Seeing a City Isn't Navigating It
posts.subtitle: 700 tasks in a real Hong Kong replica show agent perception doesn't add up to sustained action.
posts.summary: UrbanGround rebuilds a real-scale slice of Hong Kong as a closed-loop Unity sandbox and scores multimodal agents on the full trajectory they walk, not just a final answer. The result: today's agents have solid atomic perception skills, but those skills don't compose into sustained, goal-directed navigation — errors accumulate over a route, and dynamic changes like a road closure expose weak online replanning that static benchmarks never catch.

slides.title: MLLM agents can see a city. Can they navigate one?
slides.body: UrbanGround turns real Hong Kong geospatial data into a live, closed-loop sandbox and asks a harder question than any single-turn benchmark can: does perception survive a multi-step route?

slides.title: Single-turn benchmarks can't catch compounding error
bullets: Most agent benchmarks ask one-shot questions — "what's in this image," "where is X" — and never test whether a small perception mistake early in a task snowballs into a completely wrong outcome later.

Urban navigation forces exactly that: recognize a landmark, infer a destination, plan a multi-stop route under a time window, then replan when a road closes or a pedestrian steps into frame — five different skills chained in sequence, not tested in isolation.

Earlier sandboxes are either toy grid-worlds too simple to expose compounding error, or synthetic game maps that aren't grounded in a real city's actual geometry, traffic rules, and physical constraints.

slides.title: Rebuild a real city, close the loop, score the whole trajectory
slides.body: UrbanGround (from Shanghai Jiao Tong University's BCMI Lab, led by Zhuosheng Zhang, with collaborators from NUS, CUHK, and Oxford) converts territory-wide 3D geospatial data of Hong Kong into a continuously interactive Unity environment — a georegistered, physically constrained replica of a real city, not a toy grid.
bullets: Agents observe through a first-person camera and act through a compact control interface — the same observe-act loop a human would use to walk around.
Scoring is based on the actual trajectory the agent executes, not just a final answer, so errors that compound across steps get caught instead of averaged away.
700 manually verified task instances span five difficulty levels: local understanding, explicit navigation, implicit-intent inference, multi-stop planning, and dynamic replanning.
Released open-source under MIT license with web, macOS, Windows, and Linux builds, plus an OpenAI-compatible API so any model can be dropped in and evaluated.

slides.title: Where agents hold up, and where they fall apart
bullets: Local understanding and explicit navigation (levels 1-2): current MLLM agents handle these reasonably well — visual recognition and short-range spatial reasoning are solid atomic skills on their own.
Implicit-intent inference and multi-stop planning (levels 3-4): performance drops once a task demands chaining multiple inferences instead of executing one clear instruction.
Dynamic replanning (level 5): this is where agents break down hardest — a road closure or a moving pedestrian exposes weak 'online' updating, since the agent's plan was built for a static world.
Core finding: local perceptual skills don't automatically compose into sustained, goal-directed behavior — small spatial errors accumulate across a route instead of getting corrected.

slides.title: A five-step task that breaks the chain
slides.body: Ask an agent to "grab a coffee near the harbor, then get to a meeting starting in 20 minutes." It has to recognize what "near the harbor" looks like, infer which of several visible cafés fits, plan a route that fits the time window, then react when the simulation closes a road or drops a pedestrian into its path mid-route. One missed orientation cue early on compounds — the agent doesn't just answer wrong, it walks the wrong way and never recovers. A single-turn benchmark would never surface that failure.

slides.title: What the benchmark does and doesn't tell you
bullets: It's Hong Kong specifically — dense, vertical, pedestrian-heavy. Results may not transfer directly to sprawling low-density cities or indoor navigation.
The five-level hierarchy tests urban wayfinding, not every embodied-agent skill — it says nothing about manipulation, tool use, or long-horizon planning outside a city context.
700 tasks is enough for a rigorous first benchmark, but small enough that once labs start training against it, separating genuine skill gains from benchmark-specific overfitting gets harder.

slides.title: The pattern in one sentence
bullets: Perception isn't the bottleneck for embodied agents anymore — sustained, multi-step composition of that perception is.
Scoring trajectories instead of final answers catches compounding error that static QA benchmarks structurally can't see.
Dynamic, changing environments — closures, moving obstacles — are where today's agents most need better online replanning, not better recognition.

questions.prompt: What is UrbanGround's central finding about current MLLM agents?
options: They can't recognize objects or landmarks in images at all
Their local perceptual skills work fine on their own, but those skills don't compose into sustained, goal-directed behavior over longer routes
They perform worse than random guessing on every task level
They require a text-only interface to function at all
questions.explanation: Recognition and short-range spatial reasoning are solid atomic skills. What breaks down is chaining them: small errors accumulate over a multi-step route instead of getting corrected.

questions.prompt: Why does UrbanGround score the agent's full trajectory instead of just a final answer?
options: It's cheaper to compute than answer accuracy
The Unity engine requires trajectory-based scoring
Small spatial errors compound across a multi-step route — scoring only the final answer would miss failures a single-turn benchmark structurally can't see
It removes the need for a control interface entirely
questions.explanation: An agent can get the final destination right by luck after a wrong turn, or wrong despite a mostly-correct route. Trajectory scoring is what exposes compounding error along the way.

questions.prompt: Which of UrbanGround's five task levels exposes agents' weakest capability?
options: Local understanding (visual recognition)
Explicit navigation (following a direct instruction)
Dynamic replanning (adapting to road closures and moving pedestrians)
There is no meaningful difference across levels
questions.explanation: Dynamic replanning is where performance drops hardest — agents' plans are built for a static world, so a road closure or a pedestrian entering the frame exposes weak online updating that the more static earlier levels don't test.

posts.title: DPO: Skipping the Reward Model Entirely
posts.subtitle: One loss function replaces RLHF's reward model and PPO loop.
posts.summary: Direct Preference Optimization reframes RLHF as a single supervised-style loss over chosen/rejected response pairs, using the policy's own log-probabilities as an implicit reward. No reward model, no PPO rollouts, no value network — just a KL-anchored classification loss, at the cost of being strictly offline.

slides.title: RLHF works. It's also a nightmare to run.
slides.body: Reward model, PPO, a value network, four models in memory, unstable rollouts. DPO throws most of that away.

slides.title: Classic RLHF keeps four models running at once
bullets: Policy model (being trained), reference model (frozen anchor), reward model (scores completions), and usually a separate value/critic model for PPO's advantage estimate.
PPO's online rollouts mean generating text mid-training, scoring it, then updating — slow, memory-heavy, and easy to destabilize with the wrong clip range or learning rate.
The reward model is trained once on human preference pairs, then frozen — but PPO can learn to exploit its blind spots since it's only a proxy for what humans actually want (reward hacking).

slides.title: DPO's insight: the optimal policy IS a reward model
slides.body: Rafailov et al. (2023) showed that for the standard RLHF objective — maximize reward minus a KL penalty to a reference model — the optimal policy has a closed form in terms of the reward. Invert that relationship and the reward term disappears, replaced by the policy's own log-probabilities.
bullets: Substitute that closed form into the Bradley-Terry preference model — the same model used to train reward models — and the reward cancels out algebraically.
What's left is a loss computed directly from log π(chosen) and log π(rejected) under the policy and a frozen reference. No separate reward model is ever trained.

slides.title: One loss: push chosen up, rejected down, vs. the reference
bullets: Loss = -log σ( β · [ log(π(chosen)/π_ref(chosen)) − log(π(rejected)/π_ref(rejected)) ] )
β sets how far the policy may drift from the reference — small β means timid updates, large β means aggressive updates with more risk of degenerate outputs.
The reference-model ratio anchors the math: it's not 'raise the chosen probability,' it's 'raise it more than the reference already assigns.'

The training loop looks like ordinary supervised fine-tuning: batches of (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples, one forward pass each through policy and reference, one backward pass — no generation step.

slides.title: RLHF vs. GRPO vs. DPO: what each one drops
bullets: DPO trades RL's flexibility — you can reward anything you can score — for simplicity: it only works when you already have preference pairs, not a general reward signal.

slides.title: Worked example: a real refusal vs. a real answer
slides.body: Prompt: "How do I reset my router?" Chosen: a clear numbered walkthrough. Rejected: "I can't help with that."
bullets: Say the reference model already assigns log-prob -2.1 to the chosen response and -3.4 to the rejected one — a mild existing preference.
If the policy's forward pass gives log-prob -1.8 (chosen) and -3.0 (rejected), the DPO loss rewards this: both margins widened relative to the reference.
If instead the policy raised the rejected response's probability (say to -2.5), the loss penalizes it — that direction now contradicts the preference signal.
Notice no reward number is ever computed anywhere in this — the whole comparison is relative log-probabilities, which is exactly why no reward model is needed.

slides.title: Where DPO breaks: drift, bias, and a mistuned beta
bullets: Purely offline: DPO can only learn from the preference pairs you collected. If your dataset never shows a hallucination being penalized, DPO can't invent that signal the way online RL exploration in principle can.
Reference-model drift: as training proceeds, the policy can move in a direction that increases the DPO objective while degrading fluency or safety in ways the loss doesn't directly measure.
β is a real hyperparameter, not a formality — too small and the policy barely moves from the reference; too high and small datasets overfit to spurious differences between chosen/rejected pairs.

Multi-turn or long-horizon tasks don't decompose cleanly into single chosen/rejected pairs the way single-turn chat responses do — part of why RL-style methods like GRPO still get used for reasoning and agentic training.

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: DPO collapses RLHF's reward-model-plus-PPO pipeline into one supervised-style loss over (prompt, chosen, rejected) triples.
It works because the optimal RLHF policy has a closed-form relationship to the reward — invert it and the reward model becomes redundant.
Cheaper and more stable to train than PPO, but strictly offline: it can't explore beyond the preferences you already collected.
Good default for single-turn preference alignment (tone, refusals, chat quality); RL-style methods still matter for multi-step reasoning and agentic tasks.

questions.prompt: In DPO, what replaces the separate reward model used in classic RLHF?
options: A second frozen copy of the policy trained only on rejected responses
The policy's own log-probabilities, compared against a frozen reference model
A hand-written rule-based scorer
There is no replacement — DPO still trains a reward model first
questions.explanation: DPO substitutes the closed-form relationship between reward and optimal policy directly into the preference loss, so log π(chosen)/π_ref(chosen) vs. log π(rejected)/π_ref(rejected) IS the reward signal — no separate model is ever trained.

questions.prompt: What does the β term in the DPO loss control?
options: The learning rate of the optimizer
How far the policy is allowed to deviate from the reference model
The number of preference pairs per batch
The temperature used to sample rejected responses
questions.explanation: β scales the log-probability-ratio margin, acting like the KL penalty coefficient in RLHF — small β keeps the policy close to the reference, large β allows bigger, riskier updates.

questions.prompt: Which limitation is most specific to DPO compared to PPO-based RLHF?
options: DPO requires four models in memory during training
DPO needs online rollouts, which makes it slower
DPO is entirely offline, so it can't learn beyond the collected preference pairs
DPO cannot be used for chat-style alignment at all
questions.explanation: Because DPO trains on a fixed dataset of (chosen, rejected) pairs with no generation step during training, it can't explore or receive feedback on outputs outside that dataset — the opposite of PPO's online rollout loop.

posts.title: MCP Roots: The Boundary a Client Hands the Server
posts.subtitle: The one MCP primitive that flows the other way — the client telling the server where it's allowed to look.
posts.summary: Roots let an MCP client declare which directories or URIs are actually in scope for a session, so a filesystem or code-search server doesn't have to guess or hardcode paths. It's the one primitive that flows client-to-server instead of server-to-client — and it's advisory, not enforced, so it's not a substitute for real sandboxing.

slides.title: Who Tells the Server Where It's Allowed to Look?
slides.body: MCP roots let a client hand a server a short list of directories or URIs that are actually in scope for this session — instead of the server guessing, or being configured with a fixed path at install time.

slides.title: A Filesystem Server Has No Idea What 'Your Project' Means
bullets: An MCP filesystem or code-search server runs as its own process — it doesn't automatically know which folders on disk belong to the user's current workspace.
Hardcoding a path in server config breaks the moment the user opens a different project, or the editor has two or three folders open in one workspace at once.
Without a declared scope, a server is left with bad defaults: search the whole filesystem (slow and dangerous), or refuse to do anything until a human types out an absolute path.

slides.title: roots/list: the Server Asks, the Client Answers
bullets: A client that supports the feature declares a `roots` capability during initialization; a server can then send a `roots/list` request whenever it needs to know the current scope.
The client responds with an array of roots, each a `{ uri, name }` pair — typically a `file://` URI pointing at a folder the user actually has open, plus a human-readable label.
This is the one MCP primitive that runs in the opposite direction from Tools, Resources, Prompts, and Sampling: the client is exposing context to the server, not the other way around.

slides.title: The Set Can Change Mid-Session
bullets: If the client also declares the `listChanged` sub-capability, it must send a `notifications/roots/list_changed` notification whenever the user adds or removes a workspace folder.
A well-behaved server treats that notification as a cue to re-issue `roots/list`, not as data itself — the notification carries no payload, it just says 'ask again.'
This keeps the server's view of scope live without polling: it only re-checks when something actually changed.

slides.title: A Two-Folder Workspace, Then a Third Gets Added
bullets: An editor has a multi-root workspace open: `frontend/` and `backend/`. On connect, the filesystem MCP server sends `roots/list` and gets back both folder URIs with names "Frontend" and "Backend".

A search tool call now scopes its file walk to just those two directories instead of the entire home directory — faster, and it can't accidentally surface files from an unrelated project on the same machine.

Midway through the session the user adds a third folder, `shared-libs/`. The client fires `notifications/roots/list_changed`; the server re-queries, gets three roots back, and the next search call covers all three.

slides.title: Roots vs. the Other Four MCP Primitives
bullets: Roots is the odd one out: everything else pushes something from server to client (or client's model); roots pushes context from client to server.

rows: Which directories/URIs are in scope right now
Data the server exposes for the client to read
A function the model can call with arguments
A request to borrow the client's LLM

slides.title: Advisory, Not a Sandbox
bullets: The MCP spec is explicit that roots are informational: a server SHOULD respect declared boundaries, but nothing in the protocol stops a buggy or malicious server from reading outside them.
Real access control still has to happen underneath — OS file permissions, a container boundary, a chroot — because roots are just a hint communicated over JSON-RPC, not an enforcement mechanism.

Older or minimal server implementations may not query roots at all and instead rely on whatever working directory or config path they were started with — don't assume every server in the wild honors this primitive.

Skip building security guarantees on top of roots alone. Use them for scoping and relevance (faster search, less noise, fewer irrelevant results) and enforce actual isolation somewhere the server can't opt out of.

slides.title: A Hint About Scope, Sent the Other Direction
bullets: Roots let a client tell a server which directories or URIs matter right now, via `roots/list` — the only MCP primitive that flows client-to-server.
`notifications/roots/list_changed` keeps that scope current as the user opens or closes workspace folders, without the server having to poll.

Roots are advisory: they narrow what a well-behaved server searches, but they are not a security boundary — pair them with real OS- or container-level isolation for anything that actually needs to be enforced.

questions.prompt: Which direction does the Roots primitive flow, compared to Resources, Tools, and Prompts?
options: Server to client, just like the others
Client to server — the client tells the server what's in scope
It's bidirectional and negotiated per request
It flows between two servers, bypassing the client
questions.explanation: Roots is the one primitive that runs in the opposite direction: the client exposes context (which directories/URIs are relevant) to the server, rather than the server exposing something to the client.

questions.prompt: Does the MCP protocol itself prevent a server from reading files outside the roots a client declared?
options: Yes, the JSON-RPC transport blocks any request outside declared roots
No — roots are advisory; enforcement has to come from the OS, a container, or another layer the server can't opt out of
Only if the client uses HTTPS transport
Yes, but only for servers written in the reference SDK
questions.explanation: The spec says servers SHOULD respect declared roots, but nothing in the protocol enforces it. A buggy or malicious server can still read outside the declared scope, so real isolation must happen underneath.

questions.prompt: What should a server do when it receives a `notifications/roots/list_changed` notification?
options: Ignore it — the notification is purely informational and carries the new roots itself
Re-issue a `roots/list` request to fetch the updated set, since the notification carries no payload
Immediately terminate the session
Switch to Sampling to ask the client's model what changed
questions.explanation: The list_changed notification is just a signal that something changed — it doesn't include the new roots. A well-behaved server responds by calling roots/list again to get the current scope.

posts.title: LongHorizon-Harness: Trust No Round Until It's Verified
posts.subtitle: Three roles, one loop — why an agent that grades its own homework stops scaling past a few steps
posts.summary: LongHorizon-Harness wraps existing coding agents in a Manager/Executor/Auditor loop that keeps verified task state outside the model's own context, so an agent's self-reported "done" is never trusted without independent inspection. Across WeaveBench, OSWorld 2.0, and Terminal-Bench 2.1, the same backbone model and execution backend post large, measured gains purely from restructuring the loop around it.

slides.title: The model didn't get smarter — the loop did
slides.body: LongHorizon-Harness (Alibaba's AMAP-ML, arXiv 2608.01964) wraps Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or DeepSeek Harness in a three-role loop that never trusts an agent's claim of success without checking it against the real environment.

slides.title: Self-assessment breaks down over long horizons
slides.body: A single agent that plans, acts, and judges its own results in one growing context lets bad self-assessment compound.
bullets: Standard agent harnesses keep task execution, task state, and completion judgment inside one continuously-growing context
That makes state hard to track over dozens of rounds, and lets an incorrect self-assessment ("tests pass") propagate uncorrected into every later decision
The paper reframes the problem: long-horizon execution is fundamentally a task-state management problem, not just a bigger context window
Fix: keep task state explicitly outside the execution loop, and update it only with facts independently verified from the environment — not from what the executor claims

slides.title: The Manage-Execute-Audit (MEA) loop
slides.body: Three roles, three separate jobs, deliberately not shared context.
bullets: Manager: rebuilds each round from the original goal, verified progress, and prior failure evidence — decides the next bounded step
Executor: starts with a fresh context and performs exactly that one step in a desktop app or the CLI
Auditor: independently inspects the actual files, UI state, logs, and tests in the real environment — it does not trust the Executor's own claim
Only results that pass independent audit become trusted task state; a rejected result is kept as evidence for the next round's Manager, not discarded

slides.title: Model-agnostic by design
slides.body: The harness doesn't train a new model — it's an execution loop wrapped around whichever agent you already run.
bullets: Works with Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, or DeepSeek Harness as the underlying agent backend, mixed per role if you want a stronger model just for the Auditor
Manager, Executor, and Auditor can each use a different model or backend, letting you pay for quality only where it matters
A capped max_rounds (default 30) bounds how long the Manage-Execute-Audit cycle can run before stopping
Supports both GUI computer-use (clicking, typing, spreadsheets, design tools) and CLI-only work in the same continuous task

slides.title: Same model, same backend — only the loop changed
slides.body: All rows use Qwen 3.7-Plus as the backbone and Claude Code as the execution backend; the only variable is whether LongHorizon-Harness manages the loop.

slides.title: Worked example: catching a false "done"
slides.body: The Auditor's independence is the mechanism that actually prevents error propagation.
bullets: Task: migrate a repo's test suite to a new framework and confirm everything still passes
Round 12: the Executor edits the config and reports the suite is green — but its fresh context never actually re-ran the tests, it inferred success from the edit alone
The Auditor independently runs the test command and inspects the real output, finds 3 failing tests the Executor missed, and rejects the claim
That failure evidence — not a vague "try again" — feeds the next Manager round, which plans a targeted fix instead of restarting the whole task

slides.title: Tradeoffs: when the loop costs more than it saves
slides.body: Three-role verification is not free, and it isn't a substitute for a better base model.
bullets: Every round pays for a Manager call, an Executor call, and an Auditor call — 3x+ the raw token and latency cost of a single agent turn for simple, short tasks
The Auditor still trusts the environment signals it can observe; if a test itself is broken or a log can be spoofed, independent auditing doesn't catch a lie baked into the evidence
It's loop engineering, not training — a weak backbone model still writes weak code and plans weak steps; the harness only stops bad self-assessment from compounding, it doesn't fix bad judgment
For a one-shot, single-file edit, the manage/execute/audit overhead is pure waste — the gains show up on long, multi-round, verifiable tasks

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: LongHorizon-Harness treats long-horizon agent failure as a state-management problem: keep verified state outside the model, update it only from independently-audited facts
The Manage-Execute-Audit loop splits planning, fresh-context execution, and read-only auditing into separate roles that don't share the same growing context
On identical backbone (Qwen 3.7-Plus) and execution backend (Claude Code), the loop alone took WeaveBench PassRate from 51.8% to 80.7% and roughly 3×'d OSWorld 2.0 binary success
It's a wrapper, not a new model — the gains come from never trusting an agent's self-report, which costs extra rounds and only pays off on tasks long enough to actually drift

questions.prompt: What core problem does LongHorizon-Harness reframe long-horizon agent failure as?
options: A context-window size problem, solved by a bigger context
A task-state management problem, solved by keeping verified state outside the execution loop
A pure model-capability problem, solved by fine-tuning
A UI problem, solved by a better dashboard
questions.explanation: The paper's core move is treating long-horizon execution as task-state management: keep state explicit and outside the model's growing context, updating it only from independently verified facts rather than the agent's own claims.

questions.prompt: In the Manage-Execute-Audit loop, why does the Executor start each step with a fresh context instead of continuing the Manager's context?
options: To save on API costs by using a cheaper model
Fresh context keeps the Executor focused on one bounded step, while the Manager (not the Executor) carries the accumulated task history
Because the Executor and Manager must always be different models
It's a technical limitation of the underlying agent CLIs
questions.explanation: The roles are implementation boundaries, not three agents each growing their own version of history. The Executor gets a fresh context to perform one clearly defined step; the Manager alone is responsible for carrying forward verified state and failure evidence across rounds.

questions.prompt: On WeaveBench, OSWorld 2.0, and Terminal-Bench 2.1, what was held constant between the baseline and the LongHorizon-Harness result?
options: Nothing — a stronger model and backend were used for the harness results
The same backbone model (Qwen 3.7-Plus) and the same execution backend (Claude Code); only the loop around them changed
Only the benchmark task set was held constant, not the model
The harness results used no model at all, only scripted actions
questions.explanation: All reported rows use identical backbone (Qwen 3.7-Plus) and execution backend (Claude Code) for both the baseline and the harness condition, isolating the loop itself as the source of the measured gains rather than a stronger underlying model.

posts.title: Qwen3.8-Max: Alibaba's First Open-Weight Flagship
posts.subtitle: A 2.4T-parameter Max-class MoE, plus a 27B dense sibling, both landing on Hugging Face the same month
posts.summary: Alibaba's Qwen team open-sourced Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B — a 2.4-trillion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 95B active per token — marking the first time a Qwen-Max-class flagship has shipped as open weights, alongside a smaller Qwen3.8-27B dense sibling. Both build on the Qwen3.5 architecture and target coding, professional work, and long-horizon agentic reliability.

slides.title: The flagship-class weights, not just the API
slides.body: Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B is the first Qwen-Max-class model Alibaba has released as open weights, landing on Hugging Face and ModelScope in August 2026 alongside a dense Qwen3.8-27B.

slides.title: Max-class models had stayed API-only
slides.body: The open-weight community had strong mid-size models, but the true flagship tier stayed behind an API.
bullets: Qwen's own naming split "Max" (flagship, historically closed/API) from the numbered open-weight line (Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Qwen3.6)
Open developers could self-host strong 27B–397B models, but not a model built to Max-class scale — that meant no local fine-tuning, no private deployment, no weight inspection for the top tier
Qwen3.8 closes that gap by open-releasing a Max-class model for the first time, built on the Qwen3.5 architectural foundation

slides.title: What actually shipped
slides.body: Two open-weight releases, roughly a week apart, both under the Qwen3.8 name.
bullets: Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B: Mixture-of-Experts, 2.4 trillion total parameters, 95B active per token — released on Hugging Face Hub and ModelScope August 12, 2026
Qwen3.8-27B: a dense sibling, released August 14, 2026 for teams that can't host a multi-trillion-parameter MoE
Both add flexible thinking control: a tunable reasoning_effort parameter, and preserve_thinking to retain reasoning context across conversation history instead of discarding it each turn
Focus areas per the official repo: coding, professional work, research, and long-horizon agentic task completion — not just raw benchmark scores

slides.title: How teams actually run it
slides.body: Open weights mean self-hosting is real, alongside Alibaba's own hosted options.
bullets: Self-host with SGLang, vLLM, or TokenSpeed — e.g. `vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B --tensor-parallel-size 4 --max-model-len 262144 --reasoning-parser qwen3 --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`
QwenCloud offers first-class hosted access, with API compatibility for both OpenAI- and Anthropic-style request formats — a drop-in swap for existing agent code
Ships integrated into Alibaba's own tooling: Qwen Code (terminal coding agent), Qoder (agentic coding platform), and QwenWork
Quantized/local paths exist too: llama.cpp and MLX support the Qwen3.5-family architecture, and Unsloth documents running Qwen3.8 quants directly

slides.title: Qwen's open-weight line, by scale
slides.body: Qwen3.8 is the first entry in this lineage to reach Max-class parameter counts as open weights.

slides.title: Worked example: a private, self-hosted coding agent
slides.body: The open weights make a scenario possible that the API-only Max tier never allowed.
bullets: A team with strict data-residency requirements can't send a codebase to any external API, closed or not
Before Qwen3.8, their realistic self-hosted ceiling was a mid-size open model — noticeably behind flagship-tier coding quality

Now they can run Qwen3.8-27B dense on their own GPUs behind Qwen Code, or stand up Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B on a multi-node cluster if they have the hardware, with full weight access for audit or fine-tuning
Either way, nothing about the model call leaves their infrastructure — the tradeoff is entirely theirs to make between hosting cost and capability

slides.title: Tradeoffs: open weights aren't a free lunch
slides.body: "Open" and "easy to run" are different claims — read the fine print before betting infrastructure on either variant.
bullets: 95B active parameters per token is efficient relative to 2.4T total, but a MoE still needs the full expert set resident in memory to serve any request — this is not a model a single consumer GPU can host
Qwen3.8-27B dense is the realistic self-host option for smaller teams; it trades some of the Max-class ceiling for something that actually fits achievable hardware

Weights ship under a custom Qwen license (posted alongside the weights on Hugging Face/ModelScope), not a blanket MIT/Apache grant — check it before redistributing or building a commercial product on top
Qwen3.8 is explicitly built on the Qwen3.5 architectural foundation rather than a ground-up redesign — gains are targeted (coding, agentic reliability), not a wholesale architecture shift

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B is Alibaba's first Max-class model released as open weights: 2.4T total parameters, 95B active per token, on Hugging Face/ModelScope since August 12, 2026
A dense Qwen3.8-27B sibling shipped two days later for teams that can't host a multi-trillion-parameter MoE
Both add tunable reasoning_effort and preserve_thinking, and are compatible with OpenAI-/Anthropic-style APIs via QwenCloud, or fully self-hostable via vLLM/SGLang/TokenSpeed
Open weights ≠ easy hosting: the 2.4T MoE needs serious multi-GPU infrastructure, and the license is custom — check both before committing an architecture decision to it

questions.prompt: What makes Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B's release notable beyond just being a new model?

It's the first time a Qwen-Max-class flagship model has been released as open weights, not just via API
It's the first Qwen model to support coding tasks

questions.prompt: Why can't a single consumer GPU realistically host Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B, even though only 95B parameters are active per token?
options: Active parameters are recomputed from scratch on every token, which is slow on consumer hardware
A Mixture-of-Experts model must keep its full expert set resident in memory to serve any request, regardless of how few experts activate per token
The model requires a specialized TPU and cannot run on GPUs at all
Only the 27B dense variant was released with usable weights
questions.explanation: MoE reduces compute per token, not memory footprint — every expert must be loaded so any token can route to any expert. 2.4T total parameters need to fit across a multi-GPU cluster even though a given forward pass only computes through 95B of them.

questions.prompt: For a team wanting a realistic self-hosted deployment without a large GPU cluster, what does Qwen3.8 offer?
options: Nothing — only the 2.4T MoE variant was released
The Qwen3.8-27B dense sibling, released alongside the MoE flagship for smaller-scale self-hosting
A cloud-only API with no self-hosting option whatsoever
A 7B distilled version is the only self-hostable option
questions.explanation: Alongside the 2.4T-A95B MoE flagship, Alibaba released a dense Qwen3.8-27B two days later specifically sized for teams that can't host a multi-trillion-parameter MoE cluster.

posts.title: MCP Prompts: The Template Only the User Can Trigger
posts.subtitle: The third MCP primitive — not model-invoked, not app-curated, but explicitly picked by a person
posts.summary: MCP Prompts let a server ship reusable, parameterized prompt templates that a user explicitly selects — like a slash command — rather than something the model decides to call (Tools) or the app quietly attaches (Resources). A client fetches the filled-in template via prompts/get and hands the result straight to the model, so good prompting becomes something a server ships once instead of something every user has to reinvent.

slides.title: Not every good prompt should be reinvented by hand
slides.body: MCP Prompts let a server package a well-tuned prompt template once, so a user can trigger it explicitly instead of retyping a careful instruction every time.

slides.title: Good prompting doesn't scale as tribal knowledge
slides.body: The person who knows exactly how to phrase a request to a tool-rich server isn't always the one using it.
bullets: A server with a dozen Tools and Resources still needs the user to phrase the right request — "review this PR for security issues, checking auth and input validation" is easy to get vague or forget entirely
Copy-pasted prompt snippets drift out of sync as the server's capabilities change underneath them
MCP Tools are model-invoked and Resources are typically app-curated — neither primitive gives a human a direct, explicit "run this exact interaction" affordance

slides.title: Prompts: parameterized templates, explicitly picked
slides.body: A server declares a catalog of named prompts; a client turns a user's selection into ready-to-send messages.
bullets: prompts/list returns each prompt's name, title, description, and its arguments (name, description, whether required)
prompts/get takes a name plus argument values and returns a list of messages — role and content — ready to send to the model
A prompt's messages can embed resource content directly (e.g. a file's text) so the user doesn't have to manually attach anything alongside it
Servers can declare a completions capability so a client can offer autocomplete while a user types an argument value

slides.title: User-controlled — the third control plane
slides.body: MCP deliberately splits control three ways, one primitive per decision-maker.
bullets: Tools: the model decides when to call them, based on the conversation
Resources: the application typically decides what gets attached to context
Prompts: the user explicitly selects them — commonly surfaced as a slash command or menu pick in a client's UI
Because a Prompt is explicitly triggered, it's visible to the user by definition — it's not a channel for hiding instructions from them

slides.title: Worked example: /review-pr in a coding client
slides.body: A single server-defined prompt replaces a paragraph the user would otherwise retype every time.
bullets: A GitHub MCP server declares a prompt named review-pr with one argument: pr_number (required)
A user picks /review-pr from their client's command menu and enters 482
The client calls prompts/get with { name: "review-pr", arguments: { pr_number: "482" } }

The server returns messages that embed the actual diff plus a tuned instruction ("check for security issues, missing tests, and style violations") — the model receives a complete, well-formed request without the user writing a word of it

slides.title: Prompts vs. Tools vs. Resources
slides.body: Same protocol, three different jobs and three different decision-makers.

rows: May be invisible to the user

slides.title: Pitfalls: Prompts aren't a guaranteed or catch-all channel
slides.body: Support is optional, and Prompts solve a specific problem — not every prompting need.
bullets: Prompt support is an optional MCP capability; a client that doesn't implement it never shows the server's prompts at all, no matter how useful they are
Too many near-duplicate prompts clutter a picker the same way an overloaded Tools list clutters a model's decision-making — curate the catalog, don't dump every possible template into it
Required arguments should be validated by the server in prompts/get — a client shouldn't have to guess whether "pr_number" needs to be a string or an int before calling it
Prompts are for interactions a human deliberately starts; if the model itself needs to decide dynamically what to fetch or do mid-conversation, that's what Tools are for, not a Prompt

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: Prompts are MCP's user-invoked primitive: reusable, parameterized templates a person explicitly selects, distinct from Tools (model-invoked) and Resources (app-curated)
prompts/list discovers the catalog; prompts/get fills in arguments and returns ready-to-send messages, which can embed resource content directly
Because a user explicitly triggers a Prompt, it's inherently visible — it complements Tools and Resources rather than replacing either
Support is optional per client — don't rely on Prompts for anything critical unless you've confirmed your target host actually surfaces them

questions.prompt: What distinguishes MCP Prompts from Tools and Resources in terms of who invokes them?
options: Prompts are invoked by the model, just like Tools
Prompts are explicitly selected by the user — unlike Tools (model-invoked) and Resources (typically app-curated)
Prompts are invoked automatically by the server itself, with no client involvement
There's no difference — all three primitives are invoked identically
questions.explanation: MCP splits control three ways: the model decides when to call a Tool, the application typically decides what Resources get attached, and a human user explicitly selects a Prompt — commonly via a slash command or menu.

questions.prompt: What does a client receive back from a prompts/get call?
options: A raw file the user must manually copy into the chat
A list of ready-to-send messages (role and content), which can embed resource content directly
Only a boolean indicating whether the prompt exists
The full source code of the MCP server
questions.explanation: prompts/get takes a prompt name and argument values and returns a list of messages — already formed with role and content — ready to send to the model, potentially with resource content embedded inline.

questions.prompt: Why is a Prompt not a good channel for hiding instructions from the user?
options: MCP technically forbids servers from writing prompt content
A Prompt requires the user to explicitly select and trigger it, so by definition the user is aware it's being used
Prompts are encrypted and cannot contain instructions at all
Only Tools are capable of carrying instructions
questions.explanation: Since a human deliberately picks and triggers a Prompt — typically via a visible slash command or menu — the interaction is inherently visible to them, unlike a Tool call the model might make without the user noticing.
